edit_from_base: 'a deadzone so small player movements do not move the view' -> 'look-ahead in the facing direction'
prompt: Add a follow camera with look-ahead in the facing direction.

config.plan_model: Agent-tool model parameter 'sonnet' (Claude Code sub-agent; the harness did not report the resolved model id)
config.how: one fresh general-purpose sub-agent per plan, reads a job file with project brief + the developer prompt, writes numbered plan (<=8 steps, no code) via Write; not Claude Code plan mode

plans.text:
1. Review player.gd and level_01.tscn to learn how the player stores its facing direction and how movement is processed. Also check whether a Camera2D already exists anywhere in the scene tree.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node (or as a separate node that tracks it) and make it the current camera. Enable position smoothing so motion is not jarring.
3. Add exported tuning variables for look-ahead distance, look-ahead speed, and smoothing so the developer can adjust the feel in the Inspector.
4. Add a script to the camera that reads the player's facing direction each physics frame. It computes a target horizontal offset in that direction and interpolates toward it gradually.
5. Handle edge cases, such as keeping the previous look-ahead when the player is idle and avoiding rapid flipping when the player turns quickly. Consider a short delay or a deadzone before the offset changes.
6. Set camera limits from the TileMapLayer's used rectangle (or level bounds) so the view does not show empty space beyond the level edges. Make sure the look-ahead respects those limits.
7. Check that the camera works in level_01.tscn and that the enemy scenes and any UI are unaffected. Confirm the Player's sprite and collision are not affected by camera offsets.
8. Playtest by running left and right, turning, jumping, and stopping near level edges. Tune the exported values until the motion feels smooth.

1. Read player.gd and level_01.tscn to learn how the player stores facing direction, how it moves, and the level's size and layout. Confirm the project's Godot 4 version and whether a camera already exists.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node in the scene so it follows automatically, and make it the current camera. Keep it in the Player scene so every level that instances the player gets it.
3. Configure the basic follow feel on the camera: enable position smoothing with a modest speed, and optionally enable drag margins so tiny movements do not jolt the view.
4. Set camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) from the level's TileMapLayer used rectangle so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges. Decide whether this lives on the camera or is set by the level at load time.
5. Design the look-ahead: an offset applied to the camera that shifts horizontally toward the player's facing direction by a tuned distance. Smooth the transition so that turning around eases the offset instead of snapping it.
6. Implement it with a small script on the Camera2D that reads the facing direction from the player (via the existing facing variable or sprite flip state) and eases the camera offset toward the target each frame. Expose look-ahead distance and ease speed as exported variables for tuning.
7. Handle edge cases: do not flip the look-ahead when the player is idle or briefly changes direction, and reset the offset cleanly on respawn or level restart. Check that the offset does not fight with the limits or smoothing.
8. Run level_01 and playtest running, turning, jumping, and falling at both level edges. Tune the smoothing speed, look-ahead distance, and ease speed until it feels responsive without motion sickness.

1. Review player.gd and level_01.tscn to learn how the Player tracks facing direction (flip_h, a direction variable, or velocity sign) and where it sits in the scene tree.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player (or a separate node that follows it) and make it the current camera, with position smoothing enabled so movement feels fluid.
3. Expose tunable look-ahead settings (distance in pixels, smoothing speed) as exported variables so they can be tweaked in the inspector.
4. In player.gd, compute a target horizontal camera offset from the facing direction multiplied by the look-ahead distance, and interpolate the camera offset toward it each physics frame.
5. Avoid jitter when the player briefly stops or turns by keeping the last non-zero facing direction and only updating the target on real direction changes.
6. Set camera limits from the level bounds (using the TileMapLayer's used rect) so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges.
7. Run level_01.tscn and test walking left and right, turning, jumping, and stopping, then tune distance and smoothing values for comfort.
8. Check that both enemy scenes and the TileMapLayer render correctly with the camera, and that no other scene (such as a second camera) overrides the current camera.

1. Review player.gd and level_01.tscn to learn how the player stores its facing direction, how it moves, and whether any Camera2D already exists in the level or on the Player.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node so it follows automatically, and make it the current camera.
3. Enable position smoothing on the camera and tune the speed so movement feels smooth rather than rigid.
4. Add a look-ahead offset in player.gd that shifts the camera horizontally toward the facing direction, blending smoothly between left and right when the player turns.
5. Scale the look-ahead with horizontal velocity, or hold it at zero while the player is idle, so the camera does not jitter during turns or standing still.
6. Set camera limits from the TileMapLayer's used rectangle (or level bounds) so the view never shows empty space past the level edges.
7. Expose the look-ahead distance, smoothing speed, and limits as exported variables so they can be tuned in the inspector without editing the script.
8. Run level_01 and playtest running, turning, jumping, and landing near level edges, then adjust values and check that the enemy scenes and any other cameras are unaffected.

1. Open level_01.tscn and player.gd to confirm how the Player stores its facing direction and movement state, and note the level's boundaries (TileMapLayer extents) so the camera can be limited to them.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node (or as a separate node that tracks the Player) and make it the current camera, so it follows the player automatically.
3. Enable position smoothing on the camera and tune the smoothing speed so movement feels responsive but not jittery on the pixel-art tiles.
4. Expose look-ahead tuning values (distance in pixels, shift speed) as exported variables so they can be adjusted in the editor without changing logic.
5. In player.gd, expose the current facing direction (from input or the sprite's flip state) so the camera logic can read it reliably, including when the player is standing still.
6. Implement the look-ahead by smoothly shifting the camera's offset toward the facing side each frame, interpolating rather than snapping so direction changes do not cause sudden jumps.
7. Set camera limits from the TileMapLayer's used rectangle (or level-bound markers) so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges, and verify limit smoothing works with the look-ahead offset.
8. Playtest level_01 by running left, right, jumping, and turning quickly; check for jitter, over-shoot at level edges, and interaction with enemies, then tweak the exported values.

1. Review player.gd and level_01.tscn to learn how facing direction is tracked (sprite flip, a direction variable, or velocity sign) and how the Player node is placed in the level. Confirm no Camera2D already exists in the project.
2. Add a Camera2D to the Player scene as a child of the Player so it follows automatically, and enable it as the current camera. This keeps the camera working in every level that instantiates the Player.
3. Configure the camera's base behavior: turn on position smoothing with a moderate speed, and set zoom suitable for the platformer's pixel scale. Check that rotation smoothing and drag settings are left off.
4. Set camera limits from the level's bounds, using the TileMapLayer's used rectangle converted to world coordinates. This stops the camera from showing empty space beyond the ground and platforms.
5. Define look-ahead tuning values as exported variables on a small camera script: the horizontal offset distance, the speed at which the offset shifts, and an optional minimum speed before look-ahead engages.
6. Have the camera script read the Player's facing direction each physics frame and ease its offset toward the positive or negative look-ahead distance. Return the offset toward center when the player is idle, so it does not jitter on tiny direction changes.
7. Handle edge cases: the camera snaps to the player on level start, resets cleanly on respawn, and does not flip abruptly when the player turns mid-air or hits a wall.
8. Playtest level_01 by running, turning, jumping, and stopping near level edges. Tune smoothing speed, look-ahead distance, and limits until motion feels smooth and the player stays comfortably framed.

1. Review player.gd and level_01.tscn to learn how the Player moves, how facing direction is stored or derived, and whether a camera already exists in the scene.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node so it follows automatically, and enable it as the current camera.
3. Define the level bounds by setting the camera's limit values to match the TileMapLayer's used area, so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges.
4. Add exported tuning variables for look-ahead distance, look-ahead smoothing speed, and optional vertical offset so values can be adjusted in the inspector without editing logic.
5. In player.gd (or a small camera script), read the facing direction each frame and compute a target horizontal camera offset of look-ahead distance in that direction.
6. Interpolate the camera's offset toward the target using the smoothing speed, so turning around eases the view across instead of snapping.
7. Enable built-in position smoothing, and consider a small dead zone via drag margins so tiny movements and jumps do not jitter the view.
8. Playtest level_01 for edge cases like turning in place, wall collisions, falling, and respawn, then tune the exported values and confirm the camera resets correctly on respawn.

1. Review player.gd and level_01.tscn to see how the Player tracks facing direction, how it moves, and whether a Camera2D already exists. Note the level's bounds from the TileMapLayer so the camera limits can match.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node (or a separate camera node that follows it) and enable it as the current camera. Start with built-in position smoothing so movement does not feel jerky.
3. Decide how look-ahead will work: offset the camera horizontally by a set distance in the direction the player faces, and ease toward that offset instead of snapping. Expose distance and smoothing speed as exported tunable values.
4. Make player.gd report its facing direction, reusing the existing facing variable if there is one, so the camera script can read it. Keep the camera logic out of the movement code where possible.
5. Attach a small camera script that reads the player's facing direction each frame and eases the camera offset toward the target look-ahead. Hold the current offset when the player stops, so the camera does not drift back to center on idle.
6. Set camera limits from the level's TileMapLayer extents so the view never shows empty space past the edges. Check that the look-ahead offset respects those limits.
7. Handle edge cases: quick direction flips, wall contact, respawn or level load (snap the camera to the player with no smooth-in), and the enemy scenes' collisions, which should be unaffected.
8. Run level_01.tscn and playtest running, turning, jumping, and falling. Tune the distance, smoothing, and dead zone until the camera feels responsive without nausea-inducing sway.

1. Review player.gd and level_01.tscn to learn how the facing direction is stored (sprite flip, a direction variable, or velocity sign) and where the Player node sits in the scene tree. Note the level's overall bounds from the TileMapLayer.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node (or a separate camera in the level that tracks the Player), and make it the current camera. Enable position smoothing so movement feels fluid.
3. Add a small look-ahead script to the camera that reads the player's facing direction each frame. Expose the look-ahead distance and the follow speed as exported variables so they can be tuned in the Inspector.
4. Shift the camera's offset toward the facing direction by the look-ahead distance, and interpolate to the new offset smoothly so flipping direction does not cause a snap.
5. Handle edge cases, such as no look-ahead while standing idle, holding the last direction after a stop, and keeping the transition gentle during quick direction changes or wall bumps.
6. Set camera limits from the TileMapLayer's used area (or fixed values) so the view does not show empty space beyond the level edges, and confirm the look-ahead respects those limits.
7. Run level_01.tscn and test walking in both directions, turning around, jumping, and reaching the level edges. Tune the exported values until the feel is right.
8. Check the two enemy scenes and any other scenes that instance the Player for conflicting cameras, and make sure only one camera is current.

1. Review level_01.tscn and player.gd to confirm how the Player moves, how facing direction is tracked (sprite flip or a direction variable), and the level's world bounds from the TileMapLayer.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node in the scene tree (or as a separate node that follows the Player), and make it the current camera so it replaces any static view.
3. Enable position smoothing on the camera and tune its speed so movement feels smooth rather than rigidly locked to the player.
4. Create a small camera script that reads the Player's facing direction each frame and computes a horizontal look-ahead offset in that direction.
5. Smoothly interpolate the camera offset toward the target look-ahead value, so flipping direction eases the camera over instead of snapping, and ease back toward center when the player is stationary.
6. Expose look-ahead distance, ease speed, and smoothing speed as exported variables so they can be tuned in the inspector without editing the script.
7. Set camera limits from the level's TileMapLayer used rect (or fixed values) so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges, and check that look-ahead respects those limits.
8. Playtest in level_01.tscn: run, jump, and turn around repeatedly, checking for jitter, overshoot at the level edges, and enemy visibility, then adjust the tuned values.
